hero.heading: Andrea Ghidara, full stack web developer
hero.claim: Your website, cut to fit your company.
hero.subclaim: Measurements first: what you sell, and to whom. Then a site that explains, a store that sells, a platform that gets the work done.

seeking.title: The five requests I get asked most often
seeking.intro: They rarely turn up alone: a single project usually holds most of them, and deciding which to answer first is already designing it. I rewrote them, they aren't anyone's mail, but the answers are the real ones.

labels.tipo: What kind of work it is

casella.vuoto: Open one. The replies are the ones I actually write: not a quote, but where I'd start. And one in five ends with «you don't need this».

capire.oggetto: Our site doesn't reflect our direction
capire.anteprima: We have a site but the people who land on it don't understand what we actually do. We'd like to redo it, but we don't know where to start…
capire.titolo: It's almost never a wording problem.
capire.etPrima: A test you can run today, in ten minutes
capire.prima: Write down the three questions people ask you on the phone before they buy. Then open your homepage and count how many it answers in the first screenful. If it's none or one, the problem isn't how it's written, it's the order it's in: the site describes how the company is organised instead of answering the person who just arrived.
capire.tipo: The real work is deciding what comes first, not producing copy. A few weeks, and you don't need to redo the design to find out.
capire.cta: This one's mine, write to me

strumento.oggetto: One step costs us hours a week
strumento.anteprima: What we have works, but there are things we redo by hand every week. Can it be automated?
strumento.titolo: It's the only one of the five where you know if it's worth it before you start.
strumento.etPrima: The maths you can do today
strumento.prima: Hours a week, times what an hour of that person costs, times forty-five weeks. If the number that comes out isn't at least double what the tool costs, the step to automate is a different one.
strumento.tipo: A small, self-standing piece, wired into what you already use. Then it gets calibrated: how you really need it only shows once it's in use, and from there it gets taken in.
strumento.cta: This one's mine, write to me

aggiunta.oggetto: The platform is there, but it needs to do more
aggiunta.anteprima: The platform is already there and it works, but we need a couple of new things. Roughly how long would it take?
aggiunta.titolo: Almost always the platform was built for the company you were, not the one you are.
aggiunta.prima: Count how many people use it today against how many used it in the first month, and how many things it does today against how many it did. If either number has doubled, what you're asking for isn't one more feature: it's the structure underneath that has to grow with you.
aggiunta.tipo: It starts with reading, not writing: first you look at what already holds up, then you say whether what you're asking is an addition or the first piece of a new structure.
aggiunta.cta: This one's mine, write to me

fulcro.oggetto: Every morning I log into five different tools
fulcro.anteprima: Five logins, five accounts, and none of them talk to each other. We'd like one single thing, built around us…
fulcro.titolo: The problem isn't the five logins. It's that nobody knows which of the five holds the right number.
fulcro.etPrima: The number to look up twice
fulcro.prima: Take a number you need every day, open orders or active clients, and look it up in every tool where it might live. If you get two different answers, that's the job: not merging the logins, deciding which one is right.
fulcro.tipo: In stages, and the first one has to genuinely replace something. One piece that people actually use is worth more than ten that are finished and switched off.
fulcro.cta: This one's mine, write to me

nonancora.oggetto: I have an idea, but I don't know if it fits our processes
nonancora.anteprima: I have something in mind that would make our life easier, but I don't know if it's doable with what we use…
nonancora.titolo: Nobody arrives knowing whether they need a tool or a platform.
nonancora.etPrima: A question you can answer on your own, today
nonancora.prima: If one single person disappeared from the company tomorrow, what would stop? That thing is where any sensible project starts, and it's almost always the same thing costing you too much time right now.
nonancora.tipo: None, for now. Answering that question is worth more than any quote, and you don't need me to do it.

services.intro: Each one stands on its own: you can ask me for just a site, or just the automation that saves you two hours a week. But they're built to fit, and together they become the place where the work actually happens. You start with the piece that weighs most, the rest gets added when it's needed.

sites.title: Sites and landing pages
sites.description: No bought themes filled with text. It starts from what a visitor has to understand in the first three seconds; structure, words and images follow from that. Then speed and indexing: the difference between having a site and being found.

ecommerce.title: E-commerce
ecommerce.description: I connect the catalogue to what you already run (back office, warehouse, courier) instead of asking you to update two systems by hand. Payments and shipping stay configurable: tomorrow you can switch provider without rebuilding the shop.

webapp.title: Web apps and platforms
webapp.description: We start from the smallest version that stands up and put it in front of a real person early. Roles, permissions and subscriptions get built from the start: adding them later means rewriting.

ai.title: AI and automation
ai.description: Connected to your real data, not to a model that guesses. And one rule I don't negotiate: when the assistant doesn't know, it hands over to a person instead of inventing an answer.

services.stageLead: A finished website. From here on, everything underneath it.
services.blank: And yours, what is it? Write to me.
services.punch: What you call "a website" is the screen in the middle. The rest is the work behind it.
services.practice: Four pieces, and they fit together

site.title: The site
site.lead: What you see. Colour, type, hierarchy, words, images. And how all of it holds up on a six-inch screen.

logic.title: The logic
logic.lead: What the site does. Everything a visitor can do is a written rule, an edge case anticipated, an error handled before it happens.

infra.title: The infrastructure
infra.lead: What keeps it standing at three in the morning. You never see it, until it's missing. And then it's all you see.

growth.title: The services
growth.lead: What makes it grow after launch. A site going live is where the work starts, not where it's delivered.

works.title: Four problems, and how I solved them
works.intro: No logos and slogans here. You'll find the problem that existed, the decision I made, and why I rejected the easy alternative. All four come out of fifteen months at D.lab, on the company's products and its clients'.

bdroppy.name: BDroppy
bdroppy.symptom: The platform was stuck on React 14. Every new feature took weeks and the team was afraid to touch the code.
bdroppy.decision: Rewriting from scratch was the comfortable choice, but the platform had to stay online and keep selling. I chose an incremental migration, route by route, with old and new running side by side.
bdroppy.outcome: A B2B dropshipping platform now on Next.js and TypeScript, migrated without ever taking the service down.

aidify.name: Aidify
aidify.symptom: A customer support team buried under the same ten questions, repeated across five different e-commerce platforms.
aidify.decision: Not a chatbot that guesses, but one wired to the real catalogue and real orders. And above all: when it doesn't know, it hands over to a person instead of inventing an answer.
aidify.outcome: An AI-based assistant integrated across several stores, absorbing the repetitive requests and leaving the real ones to people.

customertrack.name: CustomerTrack
customertrack.symptom: Physical shops that knew nothing about their own customers: how many came in, where they stopped, what they actually looked at.
customertrack.decision: Instead of a single product, a white-label solution: each chain uses it as if it were their own. It costs more to build and pays for itself from the second customer onwards.
customertrack.outcome: An in-store behaviour analytics platform, built to be resold to several chains on the same foundation. Finished and never put online: it's the only one of the four that never had users.

visualboost.name: VisualBoost
visualboost.symptom: An editorial image library nobody could browse without sitting there waiting.
visualboost.decision: The bottleneck was the images, not the code. Before anything else: modern formats, right dimensions and progressive loading.
visualboost.outcome: An image platform for fashion, food and beauty that stays fast even on large catalogues. The public landing page was rebuilt after my work: what remains mine is the engine underneath.

process.title: Four things you get, in this order
process.intro: This isn't a list of what I do: it's what you end up holding, and when. If you don't have these four things by the end, the project isn't finished, even if the site is live.

documento.quando: Within three days of the first meeting
documento.lead: Two pages, not twenty. What has to happen for the project to have been worth anything, and what we won't do: written down, not implied.

dentro.uno: The three things that have to work, in order of importance
dentro.due: What stays out, and why it stays out
dentro.tre: The questions we can't answer yet

documento.nonlo: It isn't a quote. Numbers come later, when there is something to count.
documento.perche: If you don't recognise yourself in it, we misunderstood each other here and not in three months, when fixing it costs ten times as much.

schermo.quando: Before a single line of code exists
schermo.lead: The screens that matter, before they exist. Not all of them: only the ones where somebody decides something.

dentro.uno: The screen where someone who doesn't know you lands
dentro.due: The one where somebody buys, books or writes
dentro.tre: The one you'll use yourself, every day, for years

schermo.nonlo: It isn't finished design, and it's black and white on purpose: colour gets discussed later, order gets discussed now.
schermo.perche: We make the important decisions looking at this, together. Changing a drawing costs an afternoon; changing something already built costs a week.

link.quando: Every two weeks, until the end
link.lead: Not a screenshot and not a presentation: an address you open on your phone while the work goes on.

dentro.uno: You can click around inside it
dentro.due: You can show it to a colleague without explaining it
dentro.tre: You can reject it, which is exactly why I give it to you

link.nonlo: It isn't a release. It's the same thing, incomplete, but real: what's there actually works.
link.perche: It's the difference between finding a problem two weeks in and finding it two days from the end.

numero.quando: From launch on, with no end date
numero.lead: After launch a person answers, and the person is me. Not a ticket, not a form, not another supplier.

dentro.uno: Fixes: if I broke it, I fix it
dentro.due: Changes, quoted one at a time
dentro.tre: «Can this be done?», even when the answer is no

numero.nonlo: It isn't a support contract you have to sign. If you don't need it you don't pay for it, and if you do, you already know who to call.
numero.perche: It's why clients come back, and it's the only one of the four with no end date.

journey.title: Where I learned
journey.nota: Nobody hands you a badge when you work for yourself.

freelanceOggi.body: My own clients' projects, plus backing up other freelancers: from the dashboard that centralises a business to the small tools orbiting it.
freelanceOggi.lezione: How to talk to people who aren't technical. It's the skill I use more than any language, and the only one you can't learn by reading.

dlab.role: Front-end Developer / UI and UX Designer
dlab.body: Four products, some the company's and some its clients': a B2B platform to migrate, an AI assistant, an image archive and an analytics platform.
dlab.lezione: That a component library isn't a developer's indulgence. It's the only thing that keeps a product coherent when many people work on it, and you see it the day someone new joins.

eroi.body: E-commerce platforms across Vue and Laravel: interfaces, authentication, APIs and the panels people actually work in.
eroi.lezione: That the hard part of an e-commerce isn't the shop. It's the dashboard people work inside every day, and it's also the one nobody expects to pay for.

freelanceInizio.body: First commissioned work: development and interface for a reselling business's dashboard.
freelanceInizio.lezione: That someone else's code gets read before it gets touched. My first real job wasn't writing a new function: it was working out why whoever came before had written it that way.

client.title: Tell me what you need
client.body: Two lines are enough. I answer within 24 hours, even when the answer is no.

risposta.titolo: An answer, even if it's no
risposta.testo: Not an automated quote and not a «thanks, we'll be in touch». If it isn't work for me I'll say so, and I'll tell you who I would look for.

chiamata.testo: On the phone or on video. It is for me to understand the problem and for you to see how I think. Nothing gets sold.

preventivo.testo: What has to happen and what does not, what it costs and how long it takes. Before this there are no numbers, because there would be nothing to count.

recruiter.title: Are you considering me for a role?
recruiter.body: Then you don't need a form. Here is the up to date CV, and the two places where the code I write can actually be read instead of described.
